entry.title: Pink riverweeds spotted on a morning run
entry.content:
Behind the Observation  ·  Marathrum

Marathrum plants are riverweeds, flowering plants that live in fast-moving rivers with their roots stuck to the rocks. The genus grows from Mexico and the Caribbean to South America. Pablo Carrillo-Reyes (@pcarreyes) photographed this colony on a December morning along a river trail near Yelapa, a small beach town on the coast of Jalisco, while out for a jog with his wife. It may be Marathrum plumosum, a species found only in Mexico.

Pablo is a botany professor at the University of Guadalajara and curator of its herbarium, the Herbario Luz María Villarreal de Puga (IBUG). He has shared more than 6,400 observations of over 2,800 species on iNaturalist. Read on for his story, in his words! (Some quotes have been lightly edited for clarity.)

“I was on vacation with my family enjoying this small and beautiful beach called Yelapa. One morning my wife and I went jogging, but as always occurs, I was very distracted seeing plants and birds during the exercise time … (My wife has already resigned herself to the fact that I’m not a good sport partner.) The trail we took ran behind a nice river, and I saw a big colony of this nice and colorful aquatic plant.”

The river where Pablo found the colony

“At that moment I knew what it was, because 25 years before, when we (my wife and I) were undergraduate students, we visited the same area along with our botany professor, and he talked to us about this plant. At that time, Vanroyenella plumosa (the former name) had been described less than a decade earlier and was said to be the only endemic genus of plants to the state of Jalisco, Mexico. Additionally, we also learned that all this family of plants are indicators of good quality of water. These interesting facts ensured that I would never forget this plant. Each time I come across this plant I like to feel happy and talk about them to my students (or to my desperate wife who wants to keep running).”

The species Pablo learned about as a student was described in 1993 as Vanroyenella plumosa, the only species in its genus. A 2011 study moved it into Marathrum, and it’s now called Marathrum plumosum.

Riverweeds (family Podostemaceae) grow on stony riverbeds, mostly in the tropics. In Mexico, most species live in clean, low-nutrient rivers, and dams and pollution are among the threats they face. M. plumosum has been recorded from rivers in Jalisco and Oaxaca, and another species, Marathrum foeniculaceum, also grows in rivers near Puerto Vallarta. The iNaturalist community is still working out which one Pablo found.

“My interest in nature began when I was a little boy, when the internet probably was not even a project and getting a printed field guide was not easy … I loved to walk into the forest, grow plants, keep tropical fish, see birds, etc. Then, I studied biology and then a PhD in systematics.”

Coming around to iNaturalist

“I must be honest and tell you that at the beginning I refused to use this app. Many years ago, when the app was recently released in Mexico, there was a very renowned botany researcher and politician who came to my university to give a talk. During his talk he showed the public his mobile and said something like: ‘Herbaria and zoological collections are not necessary anymore. You can easily take a picture of the organism you are interested in, upload the picture, and then specialists will tell you which species it is.’ I was shocked.”

“I am a herbarium curator and I perceived this comment as a little aggressive … On the other hand, as a teacher I am concerned about the way human abilities and knowledge are being gradually replaced by AI … Well, some years later, some colleagues encouraged me to try the app and my perception turned.”

“I realized that iNat is a fantastic tool to learn, to share, to teach and document information on biodiversity. I am convinced that it is not an alternative to biological collections but instead a wonderful complement for them. I continue collecting, pressing, drying and identifying plants by traditional techniques, but additionally I upload many images to iNat. I also assign some homework to my students asking them to upload images of taxonomic groups we review in classes.”

Dive deeper

  • Check out more of Pablo’s plant observations.
  • See all Marathrum observations on iNaturalist. Know your riverweeds? Help identify them!
  • There are just over 1,200 riverweed observations on iNaturalist. Next time you’re near a fast-moving river in the tropics, take a look at the rocks!

entry.title: iNat Together: results and highlights
entry.content:
Exploring nature is better together

iNat Together: Find Your Nature Friends ran from September 18 through 28, and we asked one thing of everyone: bring someone. You did! iNaturalist Ambassadors hosted more than 280 events, from campus bioblitzes to blacklight moth nights, and people with no event nearby made plans with a friend and joined the open project.

Thank you to everyone who went outside with a friend, a neighbor, or a whole group of new faces. Thank you to the Ambassadors who made it happen, and to the identifiers who are helping put names to everything you found.

Tell us how it went. Whether you went to an event, went out with a friend, or didn't get a chance to take part this time, we'd love to hear from you. Take the short survey →

The results

280+

Ambassador events in 40+ countries and territories

132,000+

observations

19,800+

species

4,900+

observers

6,500+

identifiers

Over 1,000 iNat Together participants were new to iNaturalist, more than one in five of all observers! And more than 1,200 people joined the open project to take part on their own or with a friend.

Still have observations from September 18–28 to upload? It's not too late! Make sure you've joined your event's project or the open project, and they'll count.

Event highlights

Ambassadors hosted a variety of events: moth nights, bird walks, bioblitzes, fungus bioblitzes, moss bioblitzes, lake and river bioblitzes (so many bioblitzes!), guided walks, and even six-hour hikes. We loved them all, but here are a few highlights.

Veraguas, Panama

@wendybicho led a morning walk around the University of Panama's Veraguas campus, where the group found everything from insects to tent bats. As Wendy put it, "most importantly, we had a great time and made new friends."

River Trail Nature Center, Illinois, USA

About 30 people came to @wcbeckerson's talk on zombie insects at Cook County's "Party for the Preserves," then went looking for insects and fungi. The event was part of Lake Forest College's ZomBeetles project, where anyone can help find zombie beetles.

Canal Street Garden, Maadi, Cairo, Egypt

This bioblitz was sponsored by Dayma, a local environmental education organization that has built a community of nature lovers around Cairo, including around this small urban garden in the suburbs. iNaturalist Ambassadors and Dayma hosted an event for families, neighbors, and new and experienced iNaturalist users to come together and explore. True to the goals of iNat Together, @honeya and @scchaney met for the first time after following each other's observations on iNaturalist for the past year.

Southern Illinois University Carbondale, Illinois, USA

@kmtorres, @katiemharding, and @mschumm brought students, faculty, and staff to Campus Lake to try dipnetting, plankton netting, and sweep netting, and many of the students had not used iNaturalist before. The group was especially excited about water mites, "barely visible blue-green specks swimming around in our sampling pan." In their words, "Campus Lake was a whole underwater world of biodiversity for us to explore!"

Livingstone, Zambia

This Livingstone Lagoons event followed an introduction to iNaturalist talk a week earlier, both hosted by @claremateke. She said, "It is hot and dry at this time of year, so we did not expect to find much, but amazingly in a couple of hours, we managed to make nearly 150 observations of about 70 species. The team had fun trying to see what they could find, which included plants, birds, and insects. A passing chameleon that casually strolled by added some excitement to the day, especially as we discussed how to determine what sex it was!"

Powdermill Nature Reserve, Pennsylvania, USA

@andreakautz and @johnsond7 hosted a guided walk and identification event for over 20 people, including iNaturalist staff member @marissakolarosky, many folks from local environmental groups, and several new iNaturalist members! Favorite finds included lots of fungi, Red-backed and Dusky Salamanders, Beech Blight Aphids, and Honeydew Eater fungus.


Some of our favorite finds

Slender-billed Vulture (Gyps tenuirostris)

India · @rajibrudratariang

A Critically Endangered species. This observer added three Slender-billed Vulture observations during the campaign, and all three reached Research Grade.

Photo: @rajibrudratariang (CC BY-NC)

Syspastospora parasitica

Cook County, Illinois, USA · @dylantomtaylor

A fungus that grows on another insect-killing fungus. The observer called it his coolest find yet. He had read about this exact fungus in an iNaturalist project 24 hours before finding it, and asked in the comments whether that happens to anyone else.

Photo: @dylantomtaylor (CC BY-NC)

Diversibipalium dihangense

Aizawl, Mizoram, India · @onkar07

A hammerhead flatworm with only five observations on iNaturalist, including this one.

Photo: @onkar07 (CC BY-NC)

Trypanidius spilmani

Fort-de-France, Martinique · @etiennejager

A longhorn beetle with only two observations on iNaturalist, including this one.

Photo: @etiennejager (CC BY-NC)

Leroy's Grass Jumping Spider (Festucula leroyae)

Insiza, Zimbabwe · @moira_fitzpatrick

One of about ten observations of this species on iNaturalist.

Photo: @moira_fitzpatrick (CC BY-NC)

Sorcerer's Dorid (Polycera atra)

Santa Cruz, California, USA · @vireosylva

One of 74 Sorcerer's Dorids recorded during the campaign, coming primarily from the Santa Cruz Harbor Dockfouling Bioblitz and the No Bones Bioblitz in Monterey Bay.

Photo: @vireosylva (CC BY-NC)

Chilean Rosehair Tarantula

Linares, Maule, Chile · @tjbr0ss

This gorgeous tarantula is a common pet for hobbyists in North America and Europe, but its natural habitat is the high desert and scrub regions of Chile, Bolivia, and Argentina. This one was found in the Maule region of Chile.

Photo: @tjbr0ss (CC BY-NC)

Gossea corynetes

Oban Bay, Scotland · @f-sundw

One of only three observations of this small marine hydrozoan on iNaturalist. Fun fact: all three were made by this same observer in the same bay in Scotland!

Photo: @f-sundw (CC BY)

Help with identifications

A huge thank you to the more than 6,500 identifiers who have already added IDs to iNat Together observations. Your expertise is what turns a photo from a fun day outside into data that scientists can use.

About 61% of iNat Together observations still need an ID. If you know a group of organisms or a region, your identifications help observations reach Research Grade.

Ready to help? Visit the iNat Together identification page and filter for the places and taxa you know best.

Host next time

Every iNat Together event was hosted by an iNaturalist Ambassador. If you'd like to bring people together around iNaturalist where you live, the Ambassador sign-up form reopens on October 1.

Learn more about the Ambassador program →

To everyone who took part, and especially everyone who brought someone along: thank you. Every friend you introduced to iNaturalist, and every new species you noticed together, makes this community stronger. We can't wait to see where you explore next.

entry.title: A polypore expert who follows her curiosity | Identifier Profile: @arielbonkoski
entry.content:
Identifier Profile  ·  Ariel Bonkoski (@arielbonkoski)

Photo of Ariel by Brooks Bonkoski

Ariel Bonkoski (@arielbonkoski) is based in Duluth, Minnesota, where she teaches mushroom foraging and identification. She is the author of Mushrooms & Fungi For Kids and is also Co-President of the Head of the Lakes Chapter of the Minnesota Master Naturalist program.

On iNaturalist, she identifies fungi, especially polypores. @cabracrazy, who nominated her for this series, wrote: “She puts in SO MUCH WORK to ID this difficult group of fungi and deserves recognition for her efforts. We call her the Polypore Queen.”

“My interest in nature was a slow burn that was set ablaze in adulthood after discovering how cool mushrooms are! Throughout childhood, my family would go on yearly camping trips along Lake Superior. Each year, my parents would buy my sister and I various nature guides to keep us busy during these trips. We would discover fish and crayfish along the shore, hunt for rocks, and watch the seagulls.”

“It wasn’t until I was about 23 years old that I identified and foraged my first wild mushroom which quickly catapulted myself into the wonderful wild world that nature is. My interest in nature really started with mushrooms, but the more I learned about them, the more I learned about the other organisms that Fungi interact with and the more I wanted to understand other organisms in general. It eventually led me to a Co-President position in my local Minnesota Master Naturalist Program.”

“I was introduced to iNaturalist by seeing other myco enthusiasts discussing identifications on the platform. I have always been very active in the mushroom identification groups on facebook, and being on a platform where folks were more science- or nature-minded was very appealing to me.”

“When I joined in 2021, the first thing that I noticed was the lack of Fungi identifiers compared to other common forms of life. With how wild mushrooms are commonly sought after for consumption, I felt a level of responsibility in trying to correct as many identifications as I could and get common edibles to research grade. Then, as iNaturalist became a kind of home-base to document DNA-sequenced Fungi, I really love working on projects to update taxonomy as the world continues to learn more about these organisms.”

“Additionally, the data collection side of iNaturalist was extremely helpful when I authored my first book. It was really helpful in providing information on seasonality and occurrence ranges.”

Why fungi?

“In general, Fungi is my main identification focus, but I specialize in shelf mushrooms or polypores. I think Fungi still have so much mystery to them. Mycologists are constantly discovering new species and new information. Just in the 10 years that I’ve been interested in Fungi, so much information has changed. And what’s exciting about that, is so many people still have so much opportunity to make new discoveries!”

“Admittedly, my ID workflow is all over the place. My ADHD means my attention tends to move in a lot of different directions. No two days are exactly the same. Some days I’m curious about what’s growing in Australia; the next, I’m diving into Fungi in the Philippines. I follow my curiosity.”

“I rely on a mix of resources including books, websites, and direct conversation with various experts. I also like to remind folks that our understanding of Fungi is constantly changing, making newer resources especially valuable for species-level knowledge.”

“I like to ID because it’s satisfying to help folks identify their finds and learn more! The platform tends to attract people that are open to new information and that really helps make the identification experience very rewarding. I’ve also built some strong connections with other identifiers which has been very fun for me.”

“As taxonomy changes, it’s been fun to tap into other growing identifiers to get them involved in helping the community update names or correct identifications. Those identifiers sometimes also tap me into things that they are trying to tackle and it can turn into learning opportunities for both of us. Learning AND sharing knowledge have always been central to my goals with iNaturalist, and they will continue to be.”

How to make your mushroom observations easier to identify

For mushrooms, Ariel suggests:

  1. “Take clear photos of the top, underside, and side of the mushroom.”
  2. “Take a photo of the environment you found it in.”
  3. “Make notes of what you found the mushroom growing in, whether it’s sand, soil, grass, mulch, wood, etc. If it is wood, list the tree type if you can.”

→ Find some more tips for photographing fungi!

Dive deeper

  • Check out Ariel’s book, Mushrooms & Fungi For Kids
  • Want more fungus? (Who doesn’t, honestly … ) Read about some standout fungus observations:
    • A Mexican biologist comes across a parasitic fungus
    • iNat’s first observation of a Microglossum clavatum earth tongue fungus
    • A bright pink mushroom in Tasmania
    • A Japanese mycologist and a poison fire coral fungus

entry.title: Check out the improved “Explore” page in the iNaturalist iPhone app
entry.content:
The Explore page in iNaturalist is where you can go to see everything that's been observed on iNaturalist. You can find the species right near you, observations in places you love, recent sightings at future travel destinations, and see the fellow iNaturalist community members that made those observations. This has historically been easiest to do on the iNaturalist website, but now, the iPhone app has a new and improved update to the Explore page that makes it easier to browse observations even when you're away from a computer!

The new Explore page has a simpler header and one universal search that allows you to look for taxa, users, projects, and places all from the same screen. Update your iPhone app V1.2.0 234, tap the Explore button, and select the magnifying glass in the upper right corner to try it.

The new Explore page has a simpler header and one universal search.

Search by taxon, user, project, or place

You can search for any taxon, user, or project in the top search bar, then set your location in the second search bar as "nearby," "worldwide," or a specific place that's registered in iNaturalist. If you've used search on the iNaturalist website, this process will feel familiar to you.

Search for any taxon, user, or project, then set your location.

You can now also search for species you haven't seen yet in specific places. Hopefully, this makes it easier for you to search for species on your life list, plan your nature outings, and learn more about the nature near you in general!

You can now also search for species you haven't seen yet in specific places.

Saved searches

In the new Explore page, you can save any combination of filters as a saved search and return to it. Once you have a search initiated, a star button will appear — tap that to add a saved search! You can remove your saved searches from the menu or search results.

Tap the star button to save a search. You can remove saved searches from the menu or search results.

We hope that until a separate Identification page is added into the app, this will help anyone interested in identifying be able to save their most frequently used filters to access on the go more easily.

How you can try it

Update your iNaturalist iPhone app, tap the Explore button at the bottom of your screen, and select the magnifying glass in the upper right corner to try the new search functionality! You can find more details at iNat Help.

Please feel free to discuss this feature on the iNaturalist forum (this makes it easier for us to gather your feedback). You can also learn more about upcoming product improvements here.

Thank you as always for being part of the iNaturalist community!

entry.title: The new Computer Vision and Geomodel with over 1,500 new taxa
Chile's largest land snail, to scale
entry.content:
Behind the Observation  ·  Macrocyclis peruvianus

The Chilean Black Snail (Macrocyclis peruvianus) is the only living species in its genus, and the largest land snail in Chile. It’s also a snail that eats other snails, along with mushrooms. Pablo Silva Reyes (@sur_endemico) photographed this one in Parque Nacional Alerce Costero, in the Valdivian rainforest of southern Chile.

There are just over 320 observations of Macrocyclis peruvianus on iNaturalist. Pablo is based in Valdivia, where he trained as an agricultural engineer and now does environmental outreach. Read on for his story, in his words! (Some quotes have been lightly edited for clarity.)

English

“We have a large group of friends with whom we visit nature reserves in search of new species to unlock. In the case of the black snail, it was after a visit from a great friend, @chrisvaldes — who curates mushrooms on the platform — along with Juan Alarcón and @leo_hormaros34. On that occasion, while we were sampling and photographing some mushroom species in the reserve, Juan told us he’d found a black snail, so our attention turned to this specimen. That’s why we used the ruler — which we’d been using to measure small mushrooms as a scale in our photographs. We’ve seen this large snail on several occasions, but we’d never taken photos of it with a ruler to better convey the size of this forest giant.”

Español

“Tenemos un gran grupo de amigos con los que visitamos reservas naturales en busca de nuevas especies por desbloquear. En el caso del caracol negro, fue tras la visita de un gran amigo @chrisvaldes quien se dedica a curar hongos en la plataforma, además de la compañía de Juan Alarcón y @leo_hormaros34. En esa oportunidad, mientras realizábamos muestreo y fotografías de algunas especies de hongos de la reserva, Juan nos comenta que encontró un caracol negro, por lo que nuestra atención se fue a este individuo, es por eso que ocupamos la regla, la cual estábamos utilizando para medir hongos pequeños a modo de escala en las fotografías. Hemos visto en varias oportunidades este gran caracol, pero nunca le habíamos tomado fotos con una regla para que se entienda mejor la dimensión de este gigante del bosque.”

“My interest in nature began at a very young age, with a deep admiration for insects, inspired by TV shows I watched as a child, such as ‘La Ley de la Selva,’ for example. On top of that, Valdivia is a very green city, surrounded by what we call a temperate rainforest. So I was fortunate enough to grow up surrounded by many insects in my backyard, which I began collecting so I could observe them more closely. Unfortunately, this interest was set aside for quite some time, and later my professional training (agricultural engineering) led me down the path of fieldwork, where I rediscovered my passion with a deep interest in native flora, birdwatching, fungi, insects, and so on. Biodiversity in general.”

“Mi interés en la naturaleza partió desde muy pequeño, con una profunda admiración por los insectos, motivada por programas que daban en la televisión cuando era pequeño, como ‘La Ley de la Selva’ por ejemplo. A esto le debemos sumar que Valdivia es una ciudad muy verde, y está rodeada por lo que denominamos bosque templado lluvioso. Así que tuve la fortuna de crecer junto a muchos insectos en el patio, con los cuales inicié mis primeras colectas para poder observarlos más de cerca. Lamentablemente esto quedó de lado por un buen tiempo y luego mi formación profesional (Ingeniería agrícola) me llevó al camino del trabajo en campo, en donde retomé mi pasión con un profundo interés por la flora nativa, el avistamiento de aves, los hongos, los insectos etc etc. Biodiversidad en general.”

“As a true Pokémon fan, I once heard someone talk about a real-life Pokédex, which really caught my attention, so I installed the app on my phone in 2020, not knowing that it would become one of my favorite platforms. At the time, I was learning to identify native plants, and it helped me a lot. I realized that if I uploaded a species and identified it, I wouldn’t forget its name afterward, and even if I did, I knew I could look it up on my profile since I’d already seen it — it worked as a great memory aid. Then I began my foray into semi-professional photography, and that’s when I decided to upload everything I photographed. It really helped me delve into other taxonomic groups I wasn’t familiar with and also meet experts in different groups.”

“Como buen fan de Pokémon, en algún momento escuché a alguien hablar de una Pokédex real, lo que llamó mucho mi atención, por lo que instalé la app en mi celular el 2020, sin saber que se convertiría en una de mis plataformas favoritas. En ese tiempo estaba aprendiendo a identificar plantas nativas y me sirvió mucho, me di cuenta que si subía una especie y la identificaba, después no se me olvidaba su nombre, y en el caso de que fuera así, sabía que podía buscarlo en mi perfil pues ya lo había visto, funcionó como una gran ayuda de memoria. Luego empecé a mi incursión por la fotografía semi profesional y ahí fue donde me propuse a subir todo lo que fotografiaba, me ayudó bastante a adentrarme en otros grupos taxonómicos que no manejaba y también a conocer gente experta en diferentes grupos.”

Photo of Pablo by Antonia Astorga

English

“Macrocyclis peruvianus is a very interesting species; it is the largest terrestrial mollusk in Chile and plays an important role in regulating fungal populations and recycling organic matter. Together with a team led by @rodrigo_barahona_13, we conducted nighttime surveys in search of terrestrial planarians (Geoplanidae) for a study in our area, and it’s always a pleasure to come across a black snail — we’ve seen more of them on these nighttime outings than during the day.”

Español

“Es una especie muy interesante, Macrocyclis peruvianus, es el molusco terrestre más grande de Chile, y cumple un rol importante en la regulación poblacional de hongos y en el reciclaje de la materia orgánica. Junto a un equipo liderado por @rodrigo_barahona_13 realizamos monitoreos nocturnos en busca de planarias terrestres (Geoplanidae) para un estudio en nuestra zona, y siempre es un placer encontrarse un caracol negro, lo hemos visto más en estas salidas nocturnas que en el día.”

As it happens, one of the black snail’s main predators is another land planarian, Polycladus gayi.

What sharing an observation can lead to

English

“Citizen science has played a very important role in recent times. Given the limited funding and time that researchers in Chile typically have, the help provided by having more eyes on the ground is greatly appreciated — especially if they provide good photographs and observational data. Personally, a while back while conducting fieldwork in Oncol Park, Valdivia, together with a friend, @manuelcorvalan, we found a species of Cyperaceae from the genus Carex. We were specifically looking for species we couldn’t identify, and I find this group quite complex; fortunately, there are very active users who specialize in this group, such as @paulaceae and @pjimmej. When we uploaded the data, they realized it was a species not previously recorded in Chile, so this report was added to the article ‘Miscellaneous chorological, nomenclatural, and taxonomic notes on Carex (Cyperaceae) from South America, including the description of three new species’ by Muñoz-Schüler et al. 2026. This demonstrates just how useful it is to share these observations on the platform. Additionally, it’s worth mentioning that we’re currently finishing a short article on the distribution range of a species for which there is little data from Chile. Together with @javiantum, we’ve been able to collect the species in new regions thanks to a record from @elecho and an incidental observation — where we noticed the species’ presence because it was in the background of the species that was photographed for the observation! We hope to have more news soon.”

Español

“La ciencia ciudadana ha jugado un rol muy importante en el último tiempo, el poco financiamiento y tiempo que suelen tener los investigadores en Chile, hace que sea muy bien recibida la ayuda de tener más ojos en terreno y sobre todo si tienen buenas fotografías y datos de la observación. Personalmente, hace un tiempo realizando un terreno en Parque Oncol, Valdivia, junto a un amigo @manuelcorvalan encontramos una especie de cyperácea del género Carex, en particular andábamos buscando especies que no identificábamos y este grupo me parece bastante complejo, pero por suerte hay usuarios muy activos que se especializan en este grupo como @paulaceae y @pjimmej. Al subirla ellos se percataron que se trataba de una especie no registrada para Chile, por lo que se añadió este reporte al artículo ‘Miscellaneous chorological, nomenclatural and taxonomic notes on Carex (Cyperaceae) from South America, including the description of three new species’ Muñoz-Schüler et al. 2026. Demostrando lo útil de compartir estas observaciones en la plataforma. Además, cabe mencionar que hoy en día estamos terminando un pequeño artículo sobre la extensión de distribución de una especie con pocos datos de Chile, junto a @javiantum hemos podido colectar la especie en nuevas regiones gracias a un registro de @elecho y una observación incidental, en donde nos percatamos de la presencia de la especie porque estaba al fondo de la especie que fue fotografiada para la observación! Esperamos tener novedades pronto sobre esto.”

Pablo’s advice for those new to iNaturalist

English

“There are many cases like the ones I mentioned earlier, so I’d like to encourage both new and long-time users not to limit themselves to just one group. iNaturalist offers the opportunity to learn about all the biodiversity around us, and with experts in many groups, every observation counts!”

Español

“Casos como los que mencioné anteriormente hay muchos, por lo tanto, me gustaría decir a los usuarios tanto nuevos como antiguos que no se limiten solo a un grupo, iNaturalist ofrece la oportunidad de aprender de toda la biodiversidad que nos rodea, y con expertos en muchos grupos, ¡todas las observaciones suman!”

Dive deeper

  • Check out more of Pablo’s amazing photos.
  • iNaturalist is full of snails and slugs from all over the world — go and find some!
  • Two past Observations of the Week featuring South American land snails: a mighty snail found in Ecuador and a rare snail seen in Brazil.

entry.title: Four new members of the iNaturalist team
entry.content:
We have some more new faces on the iNaturalist team, now making us a staff of 26! Here’s who they are and a little about what they’re working on.

New Staff Members

Brittany Bailey, Staff Accountant

Brittany is a nonprofit accounting professional, with a background in outdoor education. She’s excited to combine her love of spreadsheets and nature in her role at iNaturalist. She holds a BA in Anthropology from James Madison University. Originally from Virginia, she now lives in Colorado with her partner and dog. She loves reading, paddling, and watching hockey, and her favorite animal is the North American river otter.

Mary Jantsch, Sr. Manager of Community Moderation & Curation

Mary is a community and operations leader who has spent over a decade building programs that help people work well together. She first came to iNaturalist as an observer, then began identifying, and recently joined the team to support the network of curators and moderators. Mary lives in San Francisco, and when she’s not click-clacking away at her keyboard, you’re likely to find her growing native plants or turning a quick walk into an unexpectedly long one.

Patricia Sazama, Computer Vision/Machine Learning Engineer

Patricia is a machine learning engineer from Maryland with over a decade of experience building ML systems. She’s a lifelong nature nerd with a soft spot for fungi and frogs, and joined iNaturalist to point her technical work toward the natural world. Outside of work, you’ll usually find her wandering the woods with her partner, toddler, and dog, converting her lawn into a wildflower meadow, or sketching landscapes with more enthusiasm than skill.

Marissa Kolarosky, Major Gifts Officer

Marissa is a nonprofit fundraising professional who brings more than a decade of experience connecting people with causes they care about. Before joining iNaturalist, she was the Assistant Director of Philanthropy at the ACLU of Pennsylvania. As a nature enthusiast and amateur mycologist, she is especially drawn to the connections that form when people get curious about the natural world. Marissa lives in Pittsburgh, PA where she can often be found hiking, foraging for mushrooms, tending to an ever-growing collection of houseplants, or exploring outside with her dogs and whatever foster rescue is staying with her at the moment.

Please help us welcome our new team members!

For most of iNaturalist’s history, a very small team has supported a very large community. We’ll continue to be a relatively small team, but we’re excited to build more staff capacity to continue supporting all of you who are part of the iNaturalist community. Thank you for making iNaturalist what it is!

entry.title: You can now search and sort through your observations on the iNaturalist iPhone app!
entry.content:
Many of you have likely been out iNatting with someone and wanted to show them one of your previous observations on the iNaturalist mobile app. Until now, searching your own observations on the app was a many-step process ... but starting today, you'll be able to easily search and sort through your observations!

Use the magnifying glass icon to search your observations and species sightings!

You can tap the new search icon in the top right of your "Me" page of the app and look up any taxon. Your observations and species tabs will filter to match. When you tap a species in the species tab, you're taken directly to all your observations of that species. There's also a new sort button in the bottom right of the "Me" page that allows you to look at your observations by date added or observed.

You can press the button in the bottom right corner of the screen to sort through your own observations and species sightings. Additionally, there is a new map view for you to easily look at where you've made your observations.

This updated functionality to the mobile app has been one of our most-requested features, and we're excited that you all get to try it out now! You can find more details about how to search and sort your observations at iNatHelp.

A few additional notes:

  • This is currently available for the new iNaturalist iPhone app.
  • Right now, this functionality won't be able to sort alphabetically or by taxonomy — iNat dynamically swaps displayed names based on geographic location and user settings, meaning a single species can have multiple conflicting, overlapping, or shifting names depending on where you view it.
  • If you'd like to access more advanced filtering for observations, please continue using the "Explore" page of the app to do so.
  • Stay tuned for even more exciting updates to the functionality of the "Me" page and the "Explore" page in the future!

Please feel free to discuss this feature on the iNaturalist forum (this makes it easier for us to gather your feedback). You can also learn more about upcoming product improvements here.

Thank you as always for being part of the iNaturalist community!

entry.title: There’s beauty in grass | Identifier Profile: @kevinfaccenda
entry.content:
Identifier Profile  ·  Kevin Faccenda (@kevinfaccenda)

Photo of Kevin by Jimmy Parker

In 2021, Kevin Faccenda (@kevinfaccenda) started walking the University of Hawai’i campus, collecting every grass he could find. Right outside the botany building, he found one that had never been recorded in Hawai’i (Urochloa glumaris), and he’s been working on grass taxonomy ever since.

Kevin studied invasive grasses for his PhD at the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa, and his main identification focus on iNaturalist is grasses of the Pacific. Read on for more about his story, in his words! (Some quotes have been lightly edited for clarity.)

“I grew up in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. My Dad is a horticulturalist, so we were always gardening together, which ignited my love for plants. In high school I joined the Nature Club run by Brian Suter and competed in the Pennsylvania Envirothon. Since I already had some experience with plants, I focused on the forestry section and learned the trees of Pennsylvania; I would go into the woods behind the school after classes with my copy of Plants of Pennsylvania and try to find as many plants as possible. From there my interests spiraled smaller and smaller into shrubs, herbs, ferns, grasses, Carex, and eventually, leafy liverworts (Cuspidatula labrifolia is an especially cool one if you’ve never heard of this group before). In college at Millersville University, I became involved with the herbarium and learned even more plants from the dried specimens. Chris Hardy is the curator there and his mentorship led directly to my focusing on more and more ‘difficult’ plants.”

“I moved to Hawai’i for graduate school and became involved with the herbaria there, especially the Bernice Pauahi Bishop Museum, which has the largest collection of Hawaiian and Pacific plants in the world. I focused my research on invasive plants and eventually found about 70 new naturalized species for the islands of Hawai’i. I did a lot of fieldwork, both for work and pleasure, and any time I ran into a species I was unfamiliar with, I collected it for the herbarium or uploaded it to iNat. I’ve since graduated and moved to Saint Louis, Missouri, where I’m excited to be living in a place with significant Carex diversity; Hawai’i only has a dozen species compared to over 100 in Missouri.”

“I chose grasses because they are the most diverse family of plants in Hawai’i, with about 300 species, many of which are poorly understood. I initially wanted to study the ecology of these grasses but switched to taxonomy, history, and biogeography. The watershed moment that locked me into grass taxonomy rather than ecology was when I started walking around the University of Hawai’i campus in 2021 collecting every grass I could find, trying to learn the common urban species. I found a new weedy species that had never been reported from Hawai’i before, Urochloa glumaris. Since it was growing directly outside of the Botany building, I realized that there was much work to do on grass taxonomy and identification and proceeded to spend several years researching exactly that.”

From lifelist to research

“I started seriously using iNaturalist when I moved to Hawai’i to learn the flora and organize my photos and field notes, which is what first brought me to the site. In Pennsylvania I mostly learned through the written flora (Plants of Pennsylvania) but the equivalent version for Hawai’i (Manual of Flowering Plants of Hawai’i) was quite out of date, missing hundreds of non-native species, making iNaturalist a more comprehensive resource for non-native plants. I learn a lot through identifying other people’s observations. I regularly encounter species I haven’t seen before, and if there are high-quality photos, there might be enough information that you can key it out — or perhaps somebody’s already identified it and you can confirm that identification and learn a new species.”

“iNat helped me learn about thousands of species, although perhaps I spend too much of my time outside photographing things now. It’s difficult to go out in the forest and leave my phone in my pocket these days since I always feel like I might get an observation of some significance if I were to get another photograph. The FOMO of not taking a photo for my iNat pokedex lifelist sometimes gets to me.”

“I also use iNaturalist data for research and have published several papers using it for new records of non-native species, correcting identifications of misapplied names in the Hawaiian flora, species distribution modeling, and updating the full checklist of vascular plants of Hawai’i. I also have a website where I have maps of every grass that occurs in Hawai’i, most of the points mapped there came from iNaturalist.”

Grass blindness

“A lot of people throw their hands up at grasses because they’re a ‘difficult group’, but so are all megadiverse families. Asters are a much larger family and often just as difficult to identify, but I don’t tend to hear people dismiss them as eagerly as they dismiss grasses. Grasses seem to carry an especially strong and persistent stigma against them. As Howard Thomas said in Grass Blindness: ‘Some plants are born invisible, some achieve invisibility, and some have invisibility thrust upon them. Grasses are a case in point.’ I’m now in a position where I can identify many grasses rather easily. If I can get some people to pay more attention to grasses because they know they can get ID help from me, then I’m accomplishing my goal of pulling the cloak of invisibility away from grasses.”

“Grasses are the most ecologically and culturally important family of plants in the world. As in Isaiah: ‘All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field.’ While I am not one to take bible verses literally, truly the majority of the calories we eat come from cereal grasses including wheat, rice, maize, oats, barley, sorghum, millet, and rye; or livestock who were fed these. There is beauty in grass and I hope more people can come to recognize it.”

How Kevin identifies

“The first resource that I usually check when I’m trying to identify a plant that I don’t personally know is the observations seen nearby on iNaturalist, using the explore page to scroll through the photos of the genus or family. Then I compare many photos for each species to get a sense of the variation within each species. If that doesn’t work, I’ll usually try a regional flora, like the Manual of the Flowering Plants of Hawai’i, Flora of China, or Weakley’s Flora of the Southeastern United States and use the dichotomous keys there. I also try to use identification keys from those regional floras to learn identification characters in case some observations on iNat are misidentified.”

“Another resource I often use is Plants of the World Online. It has a Checklist Builder feature where you can enter any country or state and get a checklist of all the plants in the family or genus you’re looking at. From there, you can kind of brute force your way through this list, looking at photos on iNaturalist, or at herbarium specimen images until you find something close. Herbarium specimen images are super valuable as there are a lot of species missing from iNaturalist from tropical regions. I especially like the Smithsonian’s database, but I will also search GBIF using the filter ‘Basis Of Record = Preserved Specimen’ to get herbarium specimen images.”

How to photograph a grass

1. Full inflorescence

2. Flower macro (spikelet side-on)

3. Whole plant & habit

4. Leaf collar & ligule

For grasses and sedges, Kevin suggests always taking photos of at least four features:

  1. “The full inflorescence of the grass. If you put your hand behind the inflorescence that usually helps smartphones to focus. The CV is actually pretty decent with grasses if you give it a clear inflorescence photo. It does very poorly with leaves however, as would be expected given the importance of flowers for grass ID.”
  2. “A macro of the flowers as close as your camera can focus sharply. For grasses, try to rotate the spikelet so you are looking at it side-on and can see the zig-zag of the overlapping lemmas.”
  3. “A photo of the whole plant showing the leaves and the inflorescence all in one to get a general size and habit reference.”
  4. “The leaf collar region including the ligule. This is where a leaf diverges from the culm of the grass (grasses don’t have stems in the way that other plants do, so we use the word culm instead).”

And also … “Bonus but often not necessary: Rhizomes or stolons if present, leaf surface, habitat/landscape.”

Check out this example of a grass observation! —>

Kevin’s advice for new identifiers

“Be bold when you identify and leave your ego at the door. I hear from a lot of people who are kind of intimidated by identifying for fear of getting something wrong. Misidentifications are inevitable; I withdraw misidentifications nearly every day based on my notifications. I really appreciate these corrections as they help me learn about characters or species I may have never recognized before. Other identifiers are also usually very helpful to explain these things and I’ve had great conversations regarding observations that I initially misidentified. And if you are confident that an ID is wrong but aren’t sure exactly what the correct ID is, adding a disagreeing ID and pushing the community taxon back to the genus, family, or even further is very valuable to reset the identification process and hopefully get the erroneous ID withdrawn.”

“Community science has extraordinary power to connect people back to nature. In a time when most people live in cities and many people don’t know an oak tree from a hickory, let alone any sort of grass-like plant, getting people to pay attention and connect to the natural world is incredibly important. Given the scale of the biodiversity crisis we’re currently experiencing as we experience the sixth mass extinction, I hope that iNaturalist will help create a new generation of biodiversity-aware people who can advocate for the ecosystems that sustain us.”

  • Browse Kevin’s observations and identifications on iNaturalist.
  • Explore his Hawai’i grass atlas — maps for every grass species in the islands, most of the data points from iNaturalist!
  • There are almost 4.5 million grass observations on iNaturalist! If you’re also familiar with grasses, here are some grass observations that could potentially be identified to a finer taxonomic level.

entry.title: Most iNaturalist records of this harvestman species come from one New Zealand ranger
entry.content:
Behind the Observation  ·  Algidia viridata ssp. bicolor

If you’re not looking closely, Algidia viridata ssp. bicolor can really vanish against moss. Sebastian Doak (@sebastiandoak) photographed this one on a February night in the Charleston Conservation Area, on the West Coast of New Zealand’s South Island.

There are 31 observations of Algidia viridata on iNaturalist. Sebastian has made 22 of them. He’s lived and worked in Paparoa National Park for about eleven years, where he’s a ranger at the visitor centre. Read on for his story, in his words! (Some quotes have been lightly edited for clarity.)

“Since my first observation of Algidia viridata in April 2020, a period where the world got a little strange for a while, I became fascinated by this animal, and how well it blends into the environment around it. With a body of only about 2x4mm and longer spindly legs, it was always a challenge to find them. Until I found that using a UV light is basically a cheat code to finding harvestmen, since so many of them fluoresce. Still, you need to know the right sort of locations to look.”

Algidia viridata does a great job of blending in with moss (there’s one in this photo!)

“On my work weekends, I usually try and get out one night if the conditions are right and try to increase my species count for my ecozone. I am always looking out for harvestmen, including this one, but once again I was trying to improve my photos of this species, so I spent a bit of time with it.”

“As a member of the neurodiverse iNat community, I wasn’t diagnosed ASD until my adult years, but clues were there pretty early, including an early childhood interest in the taxonomy of spiders — a lifelong interest that has since expanded to other groups. My mum was often in the garden, and very relaxed with all the garden critters, including not being worried about handling white-tailed spiders, a spider with a common myth of causing necrotising fasciitis. Something I now keep needing to debunk for people.”

“In high school, I never considered that studying something you enjoyed was a possibility, so I didn’t take biology, and due to certain learning challenges, didn’t manage to pass high school … I got into university under special admission. I found university so much easier than high school, being able to mostly self-direct my learning, and I completed my degree in behavioural ecology. The next six years were mostly whatever jobs I could get, including a couple years on cruise ships, before getting my first position with the Department of Conservation … I feel privileged to now have a job where I get to infodump about different species to people actively seeking information about them.”

Photo of Sebastian by Annie Gallaway

Learning about harvestmen

“Before using iNaturalist, I mostly only knew of the introduced European harvestmen in our gardens growing up, and some of the large chelicera native species in my new home on the West Coast. Then when I posted one of my harvestmen pics, I got a positive response and ID from Shahan Derkarabetian (@sclerobunus), which made me want to find more. The positivity continued, and that’s pretty much where my love for harvestmen started. Like with many invertebrates, there are still countless species to find.”

A. viridata is a Triaenonychid harvestman. The subspecies viridata runs predominantly green, and the subspecies bicolor, above, is the two-toned one.

“Ever since I left the family home, I have travelled, but since getting into iNaturalist, I build most of my trips now around trying to document various invertebrates, with a strong lean on harvestmen. Before that, I had mostly visited countries in Asia, but in the past several years I have started working my way through South American countries — Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia.”

“@tsssss is a legend for identifying South American species, often being able to identify my images as iNaturalist firsts from original descriptions from about 100 years ago. Adriano B. Kury (@adrik29) both produces a ton of research and descriptions of South American species, as well as runs an awesome project to make harvestmen research accessible through the Omnipaper project.”

“With the work of these people, I am relatively confident that some of my observations are currently undescribed genera, such as this pied harvestman with spines reminiscent of the bunny harvestman. My fave seemingly undescribed genera are these prostygnids which I found near Cosanga in Ecuador. I haven’t seen anything remotely like them.”

“I would also like to shout out Erin Powell (@erincpow) for her work building on the legacy of Ray Forster in New Zealand harvestmen. New Zealand has many interesting harvestmen, like this crazy clawed Forsteropsalis fabulosa I found near Haast.”

Sebastian’s advice for those new to iNaturalist

“Check out the website. So many times I have shown people things on the iNaturalist website and once I showed them how easy it is to navigate through and check out images and observations across groups, locations and more, many of them seemed to have their interest rekindled. There is so much more to iNaturalist than just getting identifications.”

“Ask questions. iNaturalist can be a daunting experience with mountains of information. The experience I have had when asking people for more information, and seeing their passion come through, has been inspiring. If someone is correcting you, it’s not as much them calling you out, as much as wanting to get you on the right track. Especially with the high number of neurodiverse people, sometimes the information can come across ‘sharply,’ but know that is almost always meant sincerely.”

“I very much believe in the power of community in onboarding people with a passing interest into becoming truly passionate about nature. New Zealand, like many countries, faces several pressures to ecosystems, and understanding what we risk losing is an important part of the story in gaining funding and momentum to protect the special places we have here, and anywhere. The more people who are connected with nature, the more people are inspired to look after it.”

  • There are over 478,000 harvestman observations on iNaturalist — go and find some!
